title: Copper-indium hybrid derived from indium-based metal-organic frameworks grown on oxidized copper foils promotes the efficient electroreduction of CO2 to CO
abstract: This work reports a novel and effective method for the preparation of the copper-indium bimetallic electrocatalysts by the in situ growth of indium-based metal organic frameworks on oxidized copper foils as the precursor. Compared with the oxide-derived copper and the copper-based carbon material derivative grown in situ on oxidized copper foils, the as-prepared copper-indium electrocatalyst with a self-supporting structure, high roughness factor and rich lattice defects exhibits a superior CO Faradaic efficiency of 95% and good stability for the 36-h potentiostatic test at − 0.6 V versus a reversible hydrogen electrode. Density functional theory calculations indicated that the indium atoms occupying the surface copper vacancy defects show lower free energy needed for the formation of *COOH and more difficult desorption of *H than indium atoms, supported on the perfect copper surface. Thereby, the copper-indium catalyst promotes CO2 electroreduction to CO and strongly inhibits hydrogen evolution.

Copper-indium hybrid derived from indium-based metal-organic frameworks grown on oxidized copper foils promotes the efficient electroreduction of CO2 to CO
Lulu Yan a, Wenli Su a, Xingzhong Cao b, Peng Zhang b, Yu Fan a,*
a State Key Laboratory of Heavy Oil Processing, China University of Petroleum, Beijing 102249, PR China b Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, PR China

Keywords: CO2 electrochemical reduction Indium-based metal organic frameworks Copper CO Density functional theory
A B S T R A C T
This work reports a novel and effective method for the preparation of the copper-indium bimetallic electrocatalysts by the in situ growth of indium-based metal organic frameworks on oxidized copper foils as the precursor. Compared with the oxide-derived copper and the copper-based carbon material derivative grown in situ on oxidized copper foils, the as-prepared copper-indium electrocatalyst with a self-supporting structure, high roughness factor and rich lattice defects exhibits a superior CO Faradaic efficiency of 95% and good stability for the 36-h potentiostatic test at − 0.6 V versus a reversible hydrogen electrode. Density functional theory calculations indicated that the indium atoms occupying the surface copper vacancy defects show lower free energy needed for the formation of *COOH and more difficult desorption of *H than indium atoms, supported on the perfect copper surface. Thereby, the copper-indium catalyst promotes CO2 electroreduction to CO and strongly inhibits hydrogen evolution.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The capture and conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) is an important aspect of the carbon cycle, and the electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2ER) using electricity generated by renewable energy sources such as wind and solar energies is an ideal way to convert CO2 into fuel and chemicals that is both clean and controllable [1,2]. As one of the products of CO2ER, CO can be easily separated from the electrolyte under room temperature and ambient pressure [3], and it can be used as the chemical raw material to be further transformed into various hydrocarbons and oxides through reactions such as the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis [4]. However, the preference for a single product in industrial applications is in contrast to the tendency to produce multiple products in the CO2ER due to the process in which several protons assist in multielectron transfer [5]. Moreover, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) competes strongly with the CO2ER. All of these factors make the development of CO2ER catalysts with a high activity and selectivity a particularly important need.
In the past few decades, a large number of metal catalysts have been used to reduce CO2 to CO, including Au, Ag, Pd and Zn [6]. Precious metals show good performance in the CO2ER, but their high cost limits
their application. In contrast, Zn is abundant in reserves and relatively low in price, but it can achieve a high selectivity only when the potentials are very negative relative to the equilibrium potential [7]. Cu is widely utilized in the CO2ER because of its abundant reserve and low price [8–10]. Under a mild overpotential, CO2 is mainly reduced to CO and HCOOH on a Cu electrode, and HER, as a strong competitor, decreases the selectivity of CO on Cu electrodes [11,12]. According to the reaction pathways of CO2 reduction to CO, the ideal electrocatalyst should have an appropriate adsorption strength for the key *COOH intermediate, which will promote the formation of *COOH and desorption of *CO [13]. Many measures have been taken to enhance the stability of *COOH intermediates and guide the formation of CO, such as the use of bimetallic catalysts [14,15] and changes in electrolytes (e.g., the use of ionic liquids as electrolytes [16]). These approaches bring new opportunities for the development of CO2ER.
In the electrocatalytic reaction, the surface and near-surface properties of the catalysts are very important for the adsorption and desorption of reactants and intermediates as well as their catalytic activity [17]. The surface properties and catalytic activity of bimetallic catalysts can be optimized by simply changing their surface composition. In recent reports, the Cu-based bimetallic catalysts such as CuPd,

CuAu, CuSn and CuIn not only have a high selectivity for CO but also reduce the cost [18]. In comparison with pure metal electrodes, such as Fe, Zn, Co, Ni and Cu, the bimetallic catalysts formed from In and these metals inhibit HER and improve the selectivity of the process for CO [19].
In recent years, metal organic frameworks (MOFs) with supramolecular structures linked by metal nodes and organic linkers have attracted considerable attention and widespread development [20], in addition to MOF-derived oxides with uniform metal atom doping, which have been widely used in electrocatalysis [21,22]. However, MOFs tend to agglomerate when calcined at high temperatures, which reduces their electron transport efficiency during electrochemical reactions and hinders the mass transfer efficiency of reactants and products. This problem can be avoided to a great extent by employing the in situ growth of MOFs on the substrate, because the substrate can maintain the oriented arrangement of MOF derivatives during the calcination of MOFs [23]. To date, there has been no report of indium-based MOFs grown on copper foils and applied to the CO2ER.
Based on the above analyses, this study first reports on indium-based zeolite-like metal-organic frameworks (In-ZMOFs) grown in situ on copper foils followed by calcining at high temperature to obtain a Cu-In bimetallic catalyst with abundant point defects on its surface for use in the CO2ER. The periodic arrangement of metal nodes and organic linkers in the In-ZMOFs promotes the uniform distribution of In on the surface of copper foils. The synergistic effect of Cu and In greatly improves the CO2ER performance of the as-prepared catalyst.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: 4,5-Imidazoledicarboxylic acid (H3ImDC, 97%), imidazole (99.5%), sodium hydroxide (NaOH, AR), indium nitrate hydrate (99.99%), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, AR), N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.8%) and acetonitrile (99.9%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Company. Ammonium peroxydisulfate was obtained from Beijing InnoChem. Technology Co., Ltd. Carbon dioxide (CO2, 99.999%) and nitrogen (N2, 99%) were acquired from Beijing AP BAIF Gases Industry Co., Ltd. Copper foils (0.1 mm in thickness, 99.9%) were procured from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.

sections.heading: 2.2. Characterization
sections.text: Cross sections of the electrocatalysts were acquired using a Zeiss Auriga dual beam focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy (FIBSEM) system and then were observed on an FEI Tecnai G2 F30 highresolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV. Both scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) in high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF-STEM) mode, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental maps were acquired on the TEM instrument mentioned above. The morphologies and EDS analyses of the outer surfaces of the samples were carried out on an FEI Quanta 200F scanning electron microscope (SEM). X-ray diffraction (XRD) experiments were conducted on a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer equipped with a Cu Kα radiation source operated at 40 kV and 40 mA over the angular range from 5 to 50◦. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were recorded on an ESCALAB 250 system (VG Scientific) equipped with an Al Kα radiation source with an energy resolution of 0.4 eV. The electron spin resonance (ESR) spectrum was taken with a JOEL JES-FA200 spectrometer at 77 K and micro-wave power of 0.998 mW to record the signal. To further investigate the microstructural defects in the Cu/In catalyst, the Doppler broadening of annihilation radiation (DBAR) measurements was performed using a slow positron beam with a variable energy from 0.5 to 20 keV at the University of Science and Technology of China.

sections.heading: 2.3.1. In-ZMOFs grown on Cu foil
sections.text:
The synthesis of Cu(OH)2 nanowires was performed according to the literature [24]. Each copper foil (1 cm × 2 cm) was ultrasonically cleaned with ethanol then acetone for 5 min each, followed by washing with 2 M hydrochloric acid and deionized water 3× each. Finally, each copper foil was dried with N2. Next, each clean copper foil was immersed in a mixture of 4 mL of 10 M aqueous sodium hydroxide solution, 2 mL of 1 M ammonium peroxydisulfate solution and 9 mL of deionized water for 30 min at room temperature. Each treated copper foil was washed with ethanol then deionized water 3× each, followed by drying with N2 at room temperature.
In(NO3)3⋅9H2O (0.3 g) and 0.3 g H3ImDC were dissolved and vigorously stirred in 20 mL DMF and 20 mL acetonitrile at room temperature for 1 h. Next, 1.47 M aqueous imidazole solution was added, and the solution was stirred for another 0.5 h. The as-obtained copper foil with Cu(OH)2 nanowires was immersed and stirred in the above mixture for 0.5 h and then was transferred to a 100-mL Teflon-lined autoclave and maintained in an oven at 120 ◦C for 24 h. After the autoclave was cooled to room temperature, the In-ZMOFs grown on copper foil were washed and dried with N2.

sections.heading: 2.3.2. Synthesis of Cu/In
sections.text: The as-synthesized In-based MOF grown on the Cu foil was heated from room temperature to 800 ◦C with a ramp rate of 2 ◦C/min, and the temperature was held at 800 ◦C for 1 h under a N2 atmosphere, followed by cooling to room temperature. The loading amount of the Cu-In hybrid on Cu foil was approximately 1.5 mg cm− 2. Next, the as-obtained sample was electrochemically reduced in a CO2-saturated aqueous solution at − 0.6 V vs. a reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) for 1 h followed by − 0.8 V vs. RHE for 1 h. The final product, the Cu-In hybrid derived from In MOF grown on copper foils, was denoted as Cu/In.

sections.heading: 2.3.3. Synthesis of OD-Cu
sections.text: The synthesis of oxide-derived Cu (OD-Cu) followed the same steps as that of Cu/In, except that In(NO3)3⋅9H2O was removed from the synthesis process.

sections.heading: 2.3.4. Synthesis of Cu-CMD
sections.text: Cu-based carbon material derivative (Cu-CMD) was synthesized following the same steps as Cu/In, except that 0.3 g In(NO3)3⋅9H2O was replaced with 0.241 g Cu(NO3)2⋅3H2O.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
The CO2ER was performed on a CH Instruments 760E electrochemical workstation, using a two-compartment H-cell separated by an anion-exchange membrane (DuPont, Nafion 117). The working compartment was sealed to accurately collect the gas products. The electrolyte was an aqueous solution of 0.1 M KHCO3. The volume of each chamber in the cell was 100 mL, and the actual volume of electrolyte was 52 mL. A platinum plate (2 cm × 2 cm) was used as the counter electrode, and an Ag/AgCl (3 M NaCl) electrode, as the reference electrode. During the electrochemistry process, CO2 was introduced into the cathode and controlled by a mass flow controller at a flow rate of 20 mL/ min. The solution in the cathodic compartment was purged with CO2 for at least 30 min prior to the start of electrolysis, the purpose of which was to saturate the solution (pH = 6.8). All potentials were measured against an Ag/AgCl (stored in 3 M NaCl when not in use) reference electrode and then converted to the RHE reference based on the following equation: E (vs. RHE) = E(vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.210 V + 0.0591 V × pH.
The gas-phase products were analyzed with an SP3420A gas chromatograph (GC) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) to quantify the CO concentration and a flame ionization detector (FID with a methanizer) to quantify hydrogen concentration. The HCOOH

The electrochemically active surface areas (ECSAs) of three catalysts were measured in reference to previous literature [27]. After the catalysts were reduced in 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution, the electrolyte was replaced with 0.1 M HClO4 in subsequent experiments. Cyclic voltammetry curves were recorded from − 50 to 150 mV vs. RHE at scan rates from 20 to 300 mV/s. The capacitive current densities were plotted as a function of the scan rate, giving a linear plot. The slope of the linear regression was used to determine the capacitance. The ratio of the slope/ 29 gave the roughness factor of the surface. The surface roughness factor of the electropolished Cu surface was defined as 1.

sections.heading: 2.5. Density functional theory calculations
sections.text:
Density function theory (DFT) calculations were performed with the cp2k package [28]. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) function with Grimme D3 correction [29] was used to describe the system. Unrestricted Kohn-Sham DFT was used as the electronic structure method in the framework of the Gaussian and plane waves method [30]. The molecules were described by Goedecker-Teter-Hutter (GTH) pseudopotentials [31] and DZVP-MOLOPT-GTH basis sets [32]. A plane-wave energy cutoff of 500 Ry was applied. The Cu-supported surface was constructed using a four-layer (6 × 6) Cu(111) surface with a vacuum layer of 20 Å. For the In atom doped into the Cu surface vacancy defects, Cu atoms have been replaced by In atoms. For the In4@Cu model, an In4 cluster was supported by a pristine Cu(111) surface.
The computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) approach was used to calculate the potential-dependence of reaction free energies in each elementary step involving proton-electron transfer [33]. The Gibbs free energy is calculated by:

DFT, ΔS is the change in the reaction entropy, T is the temperature (300 K), ZPE is the zero-point energy, h is Planck’s constant and ν is the frequency of the corresponding vibrational mode of the binding molecules.

sections.heading: 3.1. Preparation of the Cu/In catalyst
sections.text: As shown in Fig. 1, an In-ZMOF material with a sod-like topology was directly grown on the chemically oxidized Cu foil, which was used as the precursor for the synthesis of the Cu/In catalyst. In the first step, Cu (OH)2 nanowires with an average length of 4 µm were uniformly coated on the copper foil after chemical oxidation. Next, copper foil with Cu (OH)2 NWS was placed in the preparation solution for the In-ZMOFs and reacted under a low temperature of 120 ◦C. The white spheres with an average diameter of 184.0 nm, In-ZMOFs, are dotted on the Cu(OH)2 nanowires, which look like fine filaments coating the surface of the copper foil. Afterward, the obtained sample was heated under a N2 atmosphere and then electrochemically reduced in a CO2-saturated aqueous solution, resulting in the formation of the Cu/In catalyst. The surface morphology of the Cu/In catalyst is stripe-like, with a width of approximately 0.63 µm and a serrated convex height of approximately 0.96 µm. According to EDS analysis, the average Cu, In and O atomic contents of the Cu/In are, respectively, 69.8%, 1.3% and 28.2% before the prereduction of the Cu/In catalyst. In contrast to polycrystalline Cu [34], the oxide-derived Cu has a better CO FE in aqueous CO2ER [11], which is mainly due to the formation of active sites that strongly bind to CO when the copper oxide is electrochemically reduced to a metallic state [35]. Therefore, this oxidation/re-reduction treatment is critical for high CO selectivity. In this work, using the oxide-derived Cu as a starting substrate, the CO2ER performance of the Cu/In catalyst is expected to be improved.

sections.heading: 3.2. Characterizations of the different catalysts
sections.text:
In Fig. 2, the prominent diffraction peaks at 43.3◦(111) and 50.4◦ (200) on the three catalysts all correspond to the copper foil substrate, and the diffraction peak of Cu/In at 33.0◦ is attributed to In(101). The powders carefully scraped from the copper foils were proved to be InZMOFs with the sod-like topologies, because their XRD diffraction peaks (the inset of Fig. 2) are the same as those of other In-ZMOFs reported in the literature [36]. This result indicated that In-ZMOFs were successfully synthesized on the oxidized copper foils.
The morphology and elemental distribution of the outer surface of the Cu/In catalyst are shown in Fig. 3a–c, and those of the cross-section of the Cu/In catalyst are shown in Fig. 3d–i. The outer surface of the Cu/ In catalyst shows a banded convex distribution (Fig. 3a), in which In is uniformly distributed (Fig. 3b, c). As seen from Fig. 3d–i, there is a clear boundary between the Cu/In and the copper foil, and the outermost layer is the Cu/In mixture layer. The Cu/In mixture layer was further observed by HRTEM, imaging and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns were recorded (Fig. 3d and inset). A clear lattice fringe spacing of 0.204 nm is displayed, corresponding to Cu(111) in the Cu/ In. The identified diffraction rings at 4.8, 5.5, 7.8 and 9.2 nm− 1 correspond to the (111), (200), (220) and (311) reflections of Cu. The weak and diffuse ring at 3.7 nm− 1 corresponds to In(101). The thickness of the Cu/In in the surface of the copper foil was obtained by HRTEM imaging after the samples were sectioned by using the focused ion beam (FIB) technique. The thickness of the Cu/In is approximately 3.19 µm (Fig. 3g). According to the elemental distribution, Cu and In are well mixed in the cross section (Fig. 3e–g).
From Fig. 3i–l, a significant number of lattice defects were found in the Cu/In catalyst, including point defects [37], line defects appearing as edge dislocations [38] and plane defects such as small-angle grain boundaries [39]. Among these defects, the point defects constitute a majority of the defects observed (Fig. 3i). These defects are caused by
L. Yan et al.
Chemical Engineering Journal 412 (2021) 128718
the doping of In atoms into the oxidized copper foils and the subsequent high temperature treatment [40] of the Cu/In. Because these defects alter the balance between the original atomic forces and lead to compressive strain [41], the lattice spacing corresponding to the Cu (111) plane varies in the range of 0.212–0.218 nm (Fig. 3j–l).
Fig. 4 shows the electron spin resonance (ESR) spectrum of the Cu/In catalyst with a broad signal centered at g = 2.02, which is typical for a hole that is bound to a Cu vacancy [42,43]. To further investigate the microstructural defects in the Cu/In catalyst, the DBAR spectra were measured and characterized by the S and W parameters. The synthetic means of CuIn-1 and CuIn-2 are shown in the Supplementary Information. The incident depth of the slow positron can be calculated from the incident energy by an empirical equation [44].

The maximum penetration depth (542 nm) was calculated by using the maximum incident energy of 20 keV, corresponding to the surface layer of copper foils. The S and W parameters are defined as the ratio of annihilation events in the central low-momentum region (510.2–511.8 keV) and the two flanking high-momentum regions (505.1–508.4 keV and 513.6–516.9 keV) of the annihilation peak to the

Plots of the S parameter vs positron energy E for the samples are shown in Fig. 5(a). In the surface layer, the S parameter decreases with an increasing positron energy. The magnitude of decrease in S parameter for the Cu/In is smaller than the other samples and the value of S parameter for the Cu/In is obviously maximum, indicating that the Cu/ In has the largest numbers of defects that distribute uniformly in it. Because the change in the slope of the linear S-W relationship is closely related to the variation in the defect type, the change in the defect type can be further described by the S-W curve [45,46]. As seen in Fig. 5(b), the slopes of the S-W data for OD-Cu, CuIn-1 and CuIn-2 are approximately coincident, indicating that these samples contain the same types of defects. The slope of the line fitted from the Cu/In is slightly different from the other three samples, indicating that there are subtle differences for the types of defects between the Cu/In and the other three samples. To summarize, the Cu/In has the largest number of Cu vacancy defects which distribute uniformly in it among the four samples, and the doping of In atoms into the surface-level Cu vacancy defects brings about a slight change in the defect types.

sections.heading: 3.3. CO2ER performances of the different catalysts
sections.text:
The electrocatalytic properties of the OD-Cu, Cu-CMD and Cu/In catalysts were evaluated by cyclic voltammetry (CV) in 0.1 M KHCO3 saturated with N2 and CO2, and the results are shown in Fig. 6a. Among the three catalysts, the current density of Cu/In was the lowest in the 0.1 M KHCO3 saturated with N2, and the highest in the CO2-saturated electrolyte, indicating that the HER was strongly inhibited on the Cu/In electrode. In addition, the current density of OD-Cu in the CO2-saturated electrolyte was lower than that occurring under N2, because the electrode surface was covered by adsorbed CO molecules generated from CO2 reduction [47]. For the current density of Cu/In recorded during N2 purge, the oxidation peak at − 0.1 V vs. RHE corresponds to the oxidation of In0 to In3+ [48], and the reduction peak at approximately − 0.4 V vs. RHE corresponds to the reduction of In3+ to In0 [49]. The reduction peak at − 0.2 to 0.6 V vs. RHE of the Cu/In catalyst obtained in CO2 was lower than that obtained in N2, which can be attributed to the existence of adsorbed species on the surface of the Cu/In electrode during CO2ER [48]. As seen from Fig. 6b, the current densities of OD-Cu and Cu-CMD are similar in the range of − 0.2 to − 0.7 V vs. RHE. For the Cu/In catalyst, the reduction peak appeared at − 0.4 V vs. RHE, and the production of H2 was also significantly inhibited(FEH2 ≈ 2.84%, Fig. 7c). It is known that the standard redox potential of Cu/Cux+ or In/Iny+ is in the range of − 0.2 to − 0.6 V vs. RHE [50], such that the excess Cu and/or
L. Yan et al.
Chemical Engineering Journal 412 (2021) 128718
In is reduced, and the interaction between the Cu and In phases inhibits the HER [51]. In addition, the current density of Cu/In was higher than that of either OD-Cu or Cu-CMD, because the surface roughness of the Cu/In catalyst was twice that of OD-Cu and 1.8 times that of Cu-CMD
(Table 1). Fig. 7a–c presents how the potentials ranging from − 0.2 to − 0.7 V vs. RHE affect the FEs of OD-Cu, Cu-CMD and Cu/In. For OD-Cu, the CO FE increases from 18.45% at − 0.3 V vs. RHE to 67.95% at − 0.5 V vs. RHE and then decreases to 30.46% at − 0.7 V vs. RHE, while that of Cu-CMD increases from 24.08% at − 0.3 V vs. RHE to 60.12% at − 0.5 V vs. RHE and then decreases to 26.8% at − 0.7 V vs. RHE (Fig. 7a and b). In addition, H2 is the main product at − 0.3 V vs. RHE over OD-Cu and CuCMD, while the HCOOH FEs of OD-Cu and Cu-CMD increase slowly with the increasing overpotential below − 0.7 V vs. RHE, in accordance with the results of the Cu-based catalysts previously reported [11,12,27]. The current densities of OD-Cu and Cu-CMD are similar in the range of − 0.2 to − 0.7 V vs. RHE, and the FE trends of the products (CO, HCOOH and H2) changed with the overpotential in a similar fashion. Combining these results with Fig. 6b, it can be demonstrated that the preparation process without In has a negligible effect on the activity of Cu-based catalysts. HER is the main competitor of CO2ER. For the Cu/In catalyst, the CO FE is 38.63% and the H2 FE is 2.84% at − 0.4 V vs. RHE, due to the excess Cu and/or In reduction [52]. The H2 FE is 1.78–8.01% at the whole overpotential and the CO FE is 95% at the relatively low overpotential (− 0.6 V vs. RHE) for the Cu/In catalyst (Fig. 7c). The results indicate that CO is the only major product at the overall applied potentials for the Cu/In catalyst and the introduction of the In-ZMOF derivatives greatly enhances the ability of the Cu-based catalysts to reduce CO2 to CO.
The stabilities of OD-Cu, Cu-CMD and Cu/In are evaluated by long-
L. Yan et al.
Chemical Engineering Journal 412 (2021) 128718
term electrolysis at − 0.6 V vs. RHE in Fig. 7d–f. Although the CO FEs of OD-Cu and Cu-CMD reached 62.02% and 51.05% in the first 2 h, the CO FE of OD-Cu was drastically reduced by 22.27%, while that of Cu-CMD
remained stable at 49.43% after 10 h of operation. In addition, the CO FEs of OD-Cu and Cu-CMD decreased by 38.84% and 7.72% after 16 h, indicating the degraded stability of OD-Cu and Cu-CMD. The above
L. Yan et al.
Chemical Engineering Journal 412 (2021) 128718
results demonstrate that the stability of Cu-CMD is better than that of OD-Cu. The oxide layer in the OD-Cu surface is about 0.38 µm, while that in the Cu-CMD surface is about 2.42 µm (Fig. S1). The superior CuCMD performance should be attributed to its larger surface roughness (Table 1) and electrochemically active surface areas (Fig. S1) [27]. For the OD-Cu, the FE of CH4 is 1.3% at − 0.6 V vs. RHE, which does not exist in the products of the Cu-CMD. Compared with polycrystalline Cu, the oxide-derived Cu catalysts exhibit a better CO FE in aqueous CO2ER at lower potentials [11], which is mainly due to a large number of grain boundaries [53] and the increased local PH on the roughened Cu surface [47] formed by successive oxidation and reduction. Thus, the different product distribution is more adequately explained by the effects of local pH and morphological factors [27]. The Cu0 nanocrystals synthesized through the oxidation and re-reduction of Cu nanoparticles show a better stability in producing n-propanol over 12-h potentiostatic test in the CO2ER compared to the initial Cu nanoparticles [54]. The improved stability of the Cu0 nanocrystals is attributed to the low propensity toward CH4 formation, because the intermediates such as COHads formed during CH4 production could decompose into graphitic carbon [55]. The suppression of this route minimizes the poisoning and deactivation of the catalyst. The long-term test lead to the accumulation of the intermediates formed during CH4 production for the OD-Cu, which decompose into graphitic carbon and then blocks the catalyst surface [56]. The stability of Cu-CMD is better than that of OD-Cu due to the suppression of CH4 formation. In comparison with OD-Cu and Cu-CMD, the Cu/In catalyst shows a better long-term stability (36 h) and a higher CO FE (93% on average) for aqueous CO2 reduction (Fig. 7f). As shown in Fig. 8, the current densities of the three catalysts were almost equal in the first electrolytic run, and OD-Cu was noticeably deactivated at the fifth run. The CO FE of the Cu/In catalyst remained stable in all
electrolytic runs, consistent with the results in Fig. 7d–f. The superior performance of the Cu/In catalyst should be attributed to the unique synergy between Cu and In. The Cu-In synergistic effects in CO2ER have been studied in the previous works, but there is no clear answer to the intrinsic active site. In the work of the Takanabe group [52,57], the active sites are ascribed to the Cu-In alloys, where the In atoms occupied the Cu step sites and hindered the adsorption of H and thus inhibited the HER. Through the evolution of different Cu-In catalysts such as CuInO2, Cu/In2O3 and Cu/In(OH)3 under the CO2ER conditions, the presence of a heterogeneous nanostructure of Cu-rich cores embedded within an In (OH)3 shell-like matrix was found to be essential for the high performance [51]. The interface of Cu and In plays an essential role in determining the reaction pathway for In@Cu [58]. The In-Cu interfaces have significantly stronger *COOH stability than the In-Cu alloy in the CO2ER process, which are in agreement with the recently reported results for Au-Cu interfaces and Au-Cu alloys [59]. In this study, the DFT calculation results show that the enhanced CO selectivity of the Cu/In catalyst herein is mainly due to the significantly reduced energy needed for *COOH generation on the In-Cu interface and the successful completion of *CO desorption. The introduction of In-ZMOF derivatives in the Cu-based catalysts changes the reaction path of the Cu-based catalysts (evidenced by the following DFT calculation), reducing the accumulation of organic products during the CO2ER. As a consequence, the Cu/In catalyst is more stable than either OD-Cu or Cu-CMD.
Good stability and superior CO FE are very important qualities for the preferential application of catalysts, but most Cu-based catalysts, such as oxidation-derived Cu [11,27] and the Cu-based bimetallic catalysts [57,60], often exhibit initial deactivation characters within a few hours after the reaction. As seen from Table 2, in comparison with the Cu-based bimetallic catalysts previously reported, the Cu-In catalyst synthesized herein has a greater CO FE and better stability under a low overpotential. Among the catalysts that convert CO2 into CO, the use of the traditional bulk Zn electrode [61], which is a cheap metal, offers a poor CO FE in the aqueous phase, while the CO FE can reach approximately 80% at higher potentials (greater than − 0.8 V vs. RHE) for the optimized zinc-based catalyst, which is much lower than the CO FE of the Cu-In catalyst herein (95% at − 0.6 V vs. RHE). Among the Cu-based bimetallic catalysts whose main product is CO, the Cu-Au bimetallic catalyst can approach the activity of a pure Au catalyst at the same potential [62,63], while the Cu/In catalyst herein has a greater CO FE
L. Yan et al.
Chemical Engineering Journal 412 (2021) 128718
and a better stability at lower overpotentials than the reported Cu-Au bimetallic catalyst. In addition, the Cu/In catalyst herein shows a better reduction of CO2 to CO than the other Cu-In catalysts reported in the literature [19,57].

sections.heading: 3.4. DFT calculation
sections.text:
According to the above experimental results, In nanoparticles are evenly dispersed on the Cu surface to form a Cu/In interface with a thickness of approximately 3.19 µm. As a second metal incorporated into the Cu-based catalyst, In is responsible for enhancement of the CO2ER performance via the conversion of CO2 to CO. The DFT calculation was used to further understand how the synergistic effect between Cu and In promotes the CO2ER. The mechanism of the reaction was studied by simulating the reduction process of CO2 on a Cu-supported In island in addition to the calculation of the Gibbs free energy. Since the twodimensional In island is more stable and easier to form than the threedimensional In island, a monolayer In island model is considered [59]. Because the active crystal face of Cu(111) is more exposed on the Cu/In catalyst (Fig. 2d, inset) and is also the most stable low-index facet, it is considered that the Cu(111) face is representative of the Cu on the surface of the Cu/In catalyst. The TEM results show that both point defects (circled in Fig. 3i and j) and perfect surface areas (not circled in Fig. 3i and j) exist in the surface of the Cu/In catalyst. To have a more comprehensive understanding of the effect of Cu defects on the CO2ER, the DFT models were divided into two types: monolayer In atoms supported on a perfect Cu(111) surface (named In4@Cu) and monolayer In atoms doped into the surface-level Cu vacancy defects (referred to InCu). In KHCO3 aqueous solution, CO2 is reduced to CO mainly through the
following processes: [64]
CO2 + H + (aq) + e− = ∗COOH (9)
∗COOH + H + (aq) + e− = ∗CO + H2O (10)
∗CO + H2O = CO + H2O (11)
where the asterisk (*) represents the catalyst surface. Fig. 9 shows the Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) of CO2ER on the two DFT models and the optimal configuration of intermediates related to this mechanism. According to the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model, the working potential of CO2ER electrocatalysts is defined as the greatest electrode potential for all basic reactions. Therefore, the rate-determining step (RDS) of the CO2ER process is the activation of CO2 through the formation of *COOH intermediates, which is uphill in terms of free energy for the first proton-coupled electron transfer. It is worth noting that the ΔG required for the formation of *COOH on the InCu surface is much less than that of either In4@Cu or Cu(111), indicating that the initial potential for CO2ER is lower when In is doped into the surface-level Cu vacancy defects. From Fig. 9a, the ΔG values in the whole reaction process of CO2 conversion into CO are 0.44, 0.4 and 0.3 eV for Cu(111), In4@Cu and InCu, respectively. Thereby, for the catalytic performance of CO2ER, the effect of In doping on the defect site of Cu is better than that of In supported on the perfect surface of Cu, and the Cu facet character is the worst.
To better understand the high CO selectivity of the Cu/In, the ΔG values during the formation of HCOOH and H2 are shown in Fig. 9b and c. The free energies required for *H adsorption on In4@Cu and InCu are 0.15 and 0.17 eV, respectively, which are higher than the value of 0.09

Chemical Engineering Journal 412 (2021) 128718
eV for Cu(111), so the reactivity of the Cu/In interface for HER is lower than that of Cu facets. Since a much higher Gibbs free energy (0.5 eV) is required for the formation of *OCHO on InCu compared with In4@Cu (0.26 eV) and Cu(111) (0.23 eV), the InCu surface is proven to be less active than that of either In4@Cu or Cu(111), based on the rationale that the key step of CO2 conversion to HCOOH is the formation of *OCHO [65]. Compared with In4@Cu and Cu(111), the InCu is more likely to generate CO through *COOH and is less likely to generate HCOOH through *OCHO. The two thermodynamic models of In4@Cu and InCu sufficiently explain the fact that CO2 is more easily converted into CO on the In/Cu interface rather than the Cu facets. In summary, the DFT calculation results show that the enhanced CO selectivity of the Cu/ In catalyst herein is mainly due to the significantly reduced energy needed for *COOH generation on the Cu/In interface and the successful completion of *CO desorption. Meanwhile, the strongly adsorbed *H and *OCHO inhibit the HER reaction and the HCOOH generation. For the Cu/In catalyst synthesized herein, there are the two forms of In doped in the Cu, namely, the occupation of In atoms in the surface-level Cu-vacancy defects and the support of In atoms on the perfect Cu surface. Furthermore, the occupation of In atoms in the surface-level Cuvacancy defects has an enhanced promotional effect on the conversion of CO2 into CO and more effectively suppresses the production of HCOOH and H2.
To further understand the effect of copper vacancy defects on the stability of Cu/In catalyst, we estimate the interaction energy of In and Cu surface. The interaction energy is defined as:
Eint = 1 n [E − E(In) − E(Cu) ] (12)
where the E is the total energy of the Cu/In system, E(In) is the energy of the In system and E(Cu) is the energy of the Cu surface. The n is the number of the In atom, where n = 1 for the In-doped surface and n = 4 for the In cluster. The calculated interaction energies are − 2.018 eV for In4@Cu and − 4.757 eV for InCu, indicating a stronger interaction between the In-Cu interface for the InCu electrode. As a result, In doping on the defect site of Cu is more strongly anchored to the surface of the copper foil than that supported on the perfect surface of Cu, which enhances the stability of the Cu/In catalyst.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
A self-supported Cu/In bimetallic catalyst was prepared by the in situ growth of In-based MOFs on oxidized copper foils. Measurements of CO2ER demonstrated that the Cu/In catalyst exhibits a greater CO Faradaic efficiency (95%) at low overpotentials (− 0.6 V vs. RHE) and better stability (36 h) than either oxide-derived copper (OD-Cu) or a copper-based carbon material derivative grown in situ on oxidized copper foils (Cu-CMD). The excellent CO2ER performance of the Cu/In catalyst originates from its abundance of lattice defects and high roughness factor. In addition, compared with In atoms supported on the perfect Cu surface, In atoms occupying the surface-level Cu vacancy defects reduce the free energy needed for *COOH formation and weaken the desorption of *H and *OCHO to inhibit the evolution of H2 and the production of HCOOH, which is beneficial for CO2ER to CO. This work provides a novel method for the design and synthesis of efficient bimetallic electrocatalysts for converting CO2 to CO.
